subject: Cognitive Science
title: Confirmation Bias in Reasoning
description: One-minute skill: Confirmation Bias in Reasoning.

hook.text: You believe your team is the best. You notice every win and explain away every loss. Coincidence?

buildup.text: Confirmation bias: we search for, interpret, and remember info that confirms what we already believe.

discovery.text: It affects reasoning at every step: we ask biased questions, read selectively, and recall one-sidedly.

twist.text: Scientists aren't immune. Researchers find what they expect more often than chance would predict.

climax.text: The antidote is deliberately seeking disconfirming evidence—testing your belief, not defending it.

punchline.text: You find what you look for. So look for what opposes you.

quiz.question: What is confirmation bias?
options: Favoring information that supports existing beliefs

details.summary: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, and remember information that supports existing beliefs while ignoring contradicting evidence. It affects all stages of reasoning from hypothesis generation through evidence evaluation to memory of outcomes.
details.whyItMatters: Confirmation bias is arguably the most pervasive cognitive bias. It affects scientists, doctors, judges, and everyday thinkers equally unless actively countered.
takeaways: People seek evidence that confirms rather than challenges beliefs
Ambiguous evidence is interpreted to support existing views
Confirming memories are recalled more easily than disconfirming ones

faq.question: Can awareness of confirmation bias eliminate it?
faq.answer: Awareness helps but does not eliminate it. Even trained scientists exhibit confirmation bias. Effective countermeasures include actively seeking disconfirming evidence, considering the opposite, pre-registering predictions, and using structured decision frameworks that force examination of alternat.

faq.question: Why did confirmation bias evolve if it causes errors?
faq.answer: It may have been efficient in ancestral environments where quick, consistent action mattered more than perfect accuracy. Changing your mind slowly has survival value when most environmental patterns are stable. Confirmation bias also supports social cohesion by maintaining shared group beliefs.
